blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for NVIDIA?

paragraphs.text: The outcome turns on customer returns, utilization, margins and supply-constrained growth. Custom-chip substitution or weaker customer economics would push the view toward bear. Vera Rubin began production shipments in Q3. The November 17 results call will test its ramp, customer installations and memory costs. Buybacks can lift per-share results; diluted shares fell 1.2% in fiscal 2026, while stock-based pay adds shares.

The bear case starts at $400,000 million of revenue. Growth then falls to 30%, 5% and negative 10%, with margins declining from 48% to 45% and then 42%. The bull case starts at $430,000 million, grows by 80%, 45% and 30%, and holds margins near recent levels at 56% and then 57%. These differences reflect NVIDIA’s history of growth slowing from 114.2% to 65.5%, alongside the risk that customer payback, custom chips or supply constraints weaken demand. The latest quarter delivered $96,221 million of revenue and $59,688 million of net income. The forecast excludes $23,707 million of equity-security gains and a $711 million tax release because they are not operating earnings.

blocks.heading: How much cash does NVIDIA make after stock pay?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow subtracts capital spending from cash generated by operations. “Real free cash flow” subtracts stock pay as well, treating employee equity awards as an economic cost to shareholders. The difference matters because stock compensation transfers value to employees through additional shares.

blocks.heading: Does NVIDIA's dividend come from its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after operating the business and buying necessary equipment and intangible assets. NVIDIA can use it for buybacks, dividends, investments, acquisitions or liquidity. A buyback pays shareholders who sell and reduces the number of shares outstanding; a dividend pays shareholders directly. Because buybacks have become the larger form of return, shareholder payouts have not always matched the cash generated in the same year.

earnings.meta_description: NVIDIA's November 18, 2026 results will test its guidance, recent growth and Vera Rubin execution.
earnings.opening: NVIDIA's next results are expected on November 18, 2026. Watch whether Vera Rubin's ramp is progressing.
earnings.closing: The full memo also explains NVIDIA's business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: What has NVIDIA guided for the quarter ending in October 2026?

paragraphs.text: Management’s in-force guidance for the quarter to October 2026 is revenue of $105,840 million to $110,160 million. It calls for gross margin of 73.5% to 74.5%. Management’s preliminary outlook calls for roughly 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, while supply limits how much demand it can serve.

blocks.heading: What do NVIDIA's last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: For the quarter ended July 26, 2026, revenue more than doubled from the same quarter a year earlier. Data Center revenue reached $89.0 billion, up 117% year over year, as Blackwell Ultra infrastructure ramped. Vera Rubin had begun production shipments in the following quarter, so this result was principally a Blackwell result.

Cash from operations fell to $24,077 million from $50,344 million in the prior quarter. Free cash flow fell to $21,400 million from $48,587 million. Receivables, inventory and payment timing can make quarterly cash conversion lumpy, so the decline does not by itself show a demand reversal.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in NVIDIA's next results?

paragraphs.text: The next results call is scheduled for November 17. Investors should check whether Vera Rubin’s ramp is progressing, whether customers can install the systems NVIDIA ships and whether expensive memory reduces gross margin. NVIDIA began production shipments of Vera Rubin in Q3 and expects it to provide a meaningful share of data-center revenue in that quarter.

NVIDIA has cash and extraordinary demand, but its success now depends on delivery, customer financing, infrastructure and policy. The central question is whether all those pieces arrive together—and produce enough profitable computing work to pay for what comes next.
